extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, journalism students, newsroom practitioners, and others interested in news production and newsworthiness
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Fishman's 'bureaucratic phase' theory of newsworthiness: how newsroom routines and bureaucratic source processing determine which events become news, and the stages reporters use to detect, interpret, and assemble stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bureaucratic phase (master news value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events become news only when they pass through the administrative procedures of governmental and corporate organizations — the 'bureaucratic phase' functions as a master news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fishman's central claim: 'Occurrences which are not part of some bureaucratic phase are simply ignored.' Newsworthiness is manufactured by the intersection of newsroom routines and bureaucratic source organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-scheduled (knowability/deployability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bureaucratic events are pre-scheduled (court calendars, agency meetings, council sessions), making them knowable in advance and allowing reporters to be deployed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scheduling makes coverage efficient and predictable; reporters rely on calendars and routine meetings to plan beats and meet daily quotas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-classified (source-assigned typology)
rubrics_metrics.description: The bureaucracy assigns the event a type (e.g., felony, misdemeanor, ruling, ordinance), and the reporter inherits that classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting the bureaucracy's typology simplifies interpretation and frames the story according to institutional categories rather than independent reporter assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-evidenced (documentary outputs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bureaucratic events produce documents, transcripts, and official statements — evidence reporters can use and quote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability of documentary outputs supports objectivity rituals and reduces the time and verification burden for reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized speakers (official attribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bureaucracies provide designated officials or spokespeople who can be cited, satisfying journalistic attribution norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having an 'authorized speaker' enables reporters to follow Tuchman's objectivity ritual of attribution and lends perceived legitimacy to coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition/steady supply (beat productivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beats produce repeated, similar events that create a steady supply of stories for reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine repetition helps reporters meet constant output demands and sustain thematic storylines over time (e.g., crime coverage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection through bureaucratic outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters become aware that 'something happened' primarily via bureaucratic outputs (police blotter, court docket), not by direct observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detection is institutionalized: what is logged and released by bureaucracies is what gets onto the reporter's radar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation via bureaucratic framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters interpret events by adopting the bureaucracy's frame (e.g., police characterizing an incident as 'domestic'), inheriting official labels and meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phase privileges institutional definitions over experiential accounts and shapes the reporter's understanding of what kind of story to write.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assembly into a story (templates and house style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters assemble detected and interpreted events into publishable narratives using wire-copy templates, beat traditions, and house style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form and storytelling routines (templates, newsroom conventions) determine how information is organized and presented to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat coverage as a master filter (structural exclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beat assignment functions as a structural filter: events outside existing beats are systematically uncovered or ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an exclusionary mechanism distinct from deliberate bias—absence of routine detection leads to gaps in coverage for topics without dedicated beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bureaucratic reality over experiential reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Official categorizations (police, agencies, officials) become the working reality of news, often displacing direct experiential accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News reports tend to reflect bureaucratic definitions (e.g., crime classifications, pollution measures) rather than laypeople's experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status-quo conservatism (institutional perspective reproduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because bureaucracies define and report their activities, news systematically reproduces the perspective of established institutions, reinforcing the status quo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliance on institutional sources and routines favors established viewpoints and may marginalize dissenting or grassroots perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture of thematic trends (e.g., crime waves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cycles between bureaucratic reporting and news coverage can create perceived trends (such as a 'crime wave') that do not reflect underlying real-world frequency changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fishman's example: a 'crime wave against the elderly' in NYC news emerged from a police-press feedback loop rather than an actual spike, illustrating how themes can be manufactured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barrier for citizen/non-bureaucratic sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories originating from non-bureaucratic sources (neighbors, activists, witnesses) face higher verification costs and are less likely to be reported until a bureaucracy validates them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citizen-sourced accounts require time-consuming corroboration; the default newsroom practice is often to wait for the 'bureaucratic version' to legitimize the story.
